Follicular epithelium in a predominantly microfollicular pattern. 
While the large (approximately 5 cm) left lobe mass, described in the

 microfollicular epithelium in the absence of significant colloid or evidence

 follicular neoplasm cannot be excluded.  Further characterization requires excision.

 of cystic degeneration, raise the possibility of follicular neoplasm.  Further 
 evaluation is recommended.

The mid lobe nodule is characterized by the cytomorphologic features of classical papillary thyroid carcinoma, showing branching and papillary fragments of tumor cells with enlarged nuclei with irregular nuclear membranes and open chromatin.
 
The inferior lobe nodule shows clusters and dispersed tumor cells showing enlarged nuclei with frequent nuclear pseudoinclusions. The assessment of the nuclear chromatin characteristics is somewhat limited by the outside preparation methods. Overall, the findings are suspicious for a malignant process, with the differential including any number of neoplasms associated with nuclear pseudoinclusions. While we agree that this most likely represents papillary thyroid carcinoma, given the dispersion of the nuclei and the lack of papillary or branching architecture, we cannot entirely exclude the possibility of a medullary thyroid carcinoma. Finally, the differential also includes the rare indolent neoplasm hyalinizing trabecular tumor. This is a challenging case. For the outside slides labeled C23-1491, the ThinPrep slide shows epithelial clusters in association with rare psammomatous calcifications, cyst lining-type cells, and histiocytes amidst a background of lymphocytes. In context of the subsequently discussed outside slides labeled C23-1493, the findings are suspicious for papillary thyroid carcinoma. The cell block slide submitted for review has exceptionally scant cells, insufficient for ancillary testing. Clinical and radiologic correlation is necessary to determine whether this neck mass is associated with the thyroid or represents a metastasis.
 
For the outside slides labeled C23-1492, the ThinPrep and cell block slides show an markedly atypical follicular population in irregular sheets and papillary-type clusters associated with psammomatous calcifications and nuclear atypia, including nuclear enlargement, nuclear membrane irregularities, pinpoint micronucleoli and nuclear crowding, amidst a background of histiocytes. Although intranuclear pseudoinclusions are not readily seen, the presence of architectural (papillary-like clusters) and nuclear atypia in conjunction with the psammomatous calcifications in this case is sufficient for rendering the diagnosis of papillary thyroid carcinoma.
 
For the outside slides labeled C23-1493, I agree with the outside pathologist that the ThinPrep and cell block slides show fibrovascular cores associated with markedly atypical follicular cells showing nuclear atypia and psammomatous calcifications diagnostic for papillary thyroid carcinoma.
 
For the outside slides labeled C23-1494, the ThinPrep and cell block slides show follicular cells arranged in a predominantly microfollicular/trabecular pattern (best appreciated on the cell block) with slight nuclear atypia including mild nuclear membrane irregularities, nuclear elongation, and pinpoint micronucleoli. Although the architectural features suggest a follicular neoplasm, some nuclear features raise the possibility of an invasive follicular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma or its recently described indolent counterpart, NIFTP; definitive distinction among these entities is not possible on cytologic material.

neoplastic nuclei in this case and a definitive diagnosis will require evaluation of a histological specimen.

As stated in a recent article, "accurate FNA diagnosis of PDTC remains an elusive goal" and molecular testing is recommended "to identify PDTC related genetic alterations frequently associated with aggressive biological behavior".

DIAGNOSIS COMMENT	This is an unusual case. We have 6 smeared slides corresponding to 3 passes. Two of the passes demonstrate only bland follicular cells and some watery colloid. On the third pass, however, there are clusters of overlapping cells with enlarged nuclei
showing open chromatin. These cells are arranged in branching clusters with occasional swirling architecture. A single convincing nuclear pseudoinclusion is identified. Overall, the findings are highly suspicious for papillary thyroid carcinoma. In light
 of the minimal amount of atypical cells in the background of abundant bland follicular cells, however, the atypical cells may not be representative of the 2.8 cm lesion. In other words, this may represent an incidentally sampled papillary thyroid
microcarcinoma. Radiographic correlation will obviously be helpful. Finally, because the cells are only represented in one of the passes, negative Thyroseq results may not be entirely reliable. Only scant cells are present in the cell block material,
however I will attempt a BRAFV600E immunostain in the hopes of achieving a more definitive diagnosis.

Comment		
This is an extremely unusual case. The smears demonstrate an atypical population of follicular cells showing enlarged nuclei with fine to open chromatin, nuclear grooves, and pinpoint nucleoli, with occasional cells showing true pseudoinclusions. These cells are arranged in a microfollicular to trabecular architecture, and there are no overt papillary structures identified. Immunostains performed on the cell block material demonstrate that the lesional cells are negative for BRAFV600E, IMP3, and RAS IHC (which detects H/K/NRAS p.Q61R mutations) and shows a lack of Ki67 membranous staining.
 
Overall, the nuclear cytopathology is worrisome for papillary thyroid carcinoma, however several factors make us hesitant to assign a higher BCT category, including the lack of papillary architecture, the noted circumscription by ultrasound, and the lack of BRAFV600E alteration by immunohistochemistry. Regarding the latter point, a subset of papillary thyroid carcinomas show other alterations, including RET, ETV6, or ALK fusions, so in this case Thyroseq testing could be extremely helpful for confirming a diagnosis of papillary thyroid carcinoma. Other diagnostic considerations would include a follicular neoplasm (ie follicular adenoma/follicular carcinoma), however nuclear pseudoinclusions would be extremely unusual for such tumors. Finally, we considered the possibility of a hyalinizing trabecular tumor (HTT), however the lack of hyaline-type stroma and the lack of Ki67 membranous staining both argue against this possibility. Still, HTTs have been found to harbor their own consistent molecular alterations (GLIS fusions) which would be detectable by Thyroseq.
 
In summary, the findings are compatible with a neoplastic proliferation and could be compatible with papillary thyroid carcinoma, though the differential would still include other follicular neoplasms. Given the unusual characteristics in this case, we feel it is prudent to defer to the pending molecular findings for guiding management, the results of which will be issued separately.
 
This case was reviewed with Dr. Kartik Viswanathan, who concurs with the above interpretation.

Electronically signed by Lubin, Daniel Joseph, MD on 2/1/2023 at 1728
Comment	
Both the core biopsy and the cytology specimen demonstrate high-grade epithelioid to spindled malignant cells demonstrating pleomorphic nuclei with anisonucleosis, high N:C ratio, prominent nucleoli, and variably coarse to open chromatin.  In the core biopsy specimen, the cells are found growing in sheets.  Scattered neutrophils and lymphocytes are present in the background.  Also present in the core biopsy material are papillary structures lined by tumor cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and enlarged nuclei with fine chromatin and nuclear pseudoinclusions.
 
Immunostains performed at the outside institution and reviewed at Emory demonstrate the following immunoprofile for the high-grade malignant cells:
OSCAR              Positive
CK7                   Positive
TTF-1                 Positive (patchy)
PAX8                 Rare positive cells
CK5/6                Rare positive cells
P40                    Rare positive cells
CK20                 Negative
S100                  Negative
Desmin              Negative
 
The papillary tumor cells stain are positive for CK7, TTF-1, and PAX8, essentially confirming a diagnosis of papillary thyroid carcinoma.
 
Overall, given the presence of a high grade spindled to epithelioid malignancy in association with papillary thyroid carcinoma, the findings favor an anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. The immunophenotype in this case is somewhat unusual, as TTF-1 is typically lost in ATC while PAX8 may be preserved. I also note that the thyroid gland itself does not show dominant masses. Still, in the absence of any known malignancy elsewhere, and given the association with what is morphologically and immunophenotypically compatible with papillary thyroid carcinoma, the findings favor anaplastic tranformation of a metastatic focus of PTC. Correlate with the findings of the resection specimen.

DIAGNOSIS COMMENT	
	
The smears have adequate cellularity and show clusters and isolated cells with abundant granular oncocytic cytoplasm, enlarged, occasionally bizarre, nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Histologic sections of the core biopsy material show similar findings of
an infiltrative high-grade carcinoma with oncocytic features and scattered bizarre nuclear atypia. Necrosis is identified and several mitotic figures are noted, including scattered atypical forms.

Immunostains performed on the sampled tissue demonstrate the following in tumor cells:

STAIN               RESULT
PAX-8               Positive
TTF-1               Positive
Thyroglobulin           Patchy positive
B-Raf V600E          Negative
TFE-3               Nuclear staining of unclear significance
HMB-45               Negative
Smooth Muscle Actin     Negative
Melan-A               Negative
Synaptophysin          Negative
Oct 3/4               Negative

An immunostain for RAS Q61R is pending and will be reported in an addendum.

The immunophenotype supports that the high-grade carcinoma is thyroid in origin. In the context of oncocytic cells, the bizarre nuclear atypia could represent endocrine atypia (due to retention of TTF-1 expression and patchy thyroglobulin staining);
however, due to the presence of atypical mitotic forms, scattered bizarre nuclear atypia, and the heterogeneous thyroglobulin staining, an evolving anaplastic component cannot be completely excluded, especially given the radiologic impression of the
thyroid mass, where the current sampling may not be entirely representative of the lesion. Nonetheless, the current histologic findings are in keeping for at least a poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma with oncocytic features. There should be
sufficient residual material on the core biopsy and cell block material should molecular testing be sought (>500 tumor cells, >80% tumor fraction on core biopsy material; ~250 tumor cells, >80% tumor fraction on cell block).

This challenging case was reviewed together with Dr. Melinda Lewis and Dr. Daniel Lubin who concur with the diagnosis.

pathology_extended:
- Suspicious. Cytologic features worrisome for a Hurthle cell neoplasm (see comment).
EXPERT CONSULTANT'S COMMENT: I agree with your assessment in this challenging case.
As you noted, this is a challenging case and represents one of the diagnostic pitfalls of thyroid aspiration interpretation. Specifically, when a patient has multiple nodules and the cellularity of one of the aspirates is reasonable enough to view as
suspicious for a Hurthle cell or follicular neoplasm, the question becomes when to classify the aspirate as such and recommend surgical intervention. In my opinion, I would be more comfortable classifying this aspirate as suspicious for a Hurthle cell
neoplasm from the right superior nodule for a few reasons. First, given the fact the patient has already had one aspirate that was classified as suspicious for Hurthle cell neoplasm in 2013 indicates that the nodule is cellular enough to view as a
possible neoplasm. I do not know if the nodule has grown in size or remained stable. However, this current aspirate is reasonably cellular with a pure population of Hurthle cells with minimal, if any, colloid, and also small amounts of fibrous tissue
with chronic inflammation. If the patient has clinical evidence of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, the ratio of Hurthle cells to inflammation in the superior nodule aspirate is skewed markedly toward the Hurthle cell population. As such, it is reasonable to
view the aspirate as suspicious and recommend surgical intervention.

The other aspirate from the inferior nodule is almost acellular on the smear slides but, as you noted, does have a fair number of follicular cells on the ThinPrep slides. As I have probably mentioned before, I am not a big proponent of ThinPrep cytology
in the setting of thyroid FNA procedures. When the methodology was introduced over 10 years ago for cervical/vaginal cytology, the purpose was essentially three-fold in that setting, but those reasons in the context of thyroid cytology are actually more
detrimental to appropriate interpretation.
Specifically, this approach is fluid conservative so that if molecular testing is required, there is fluid remaining for such a procedure. However, in a low prevalence state of malignancy, molecular cytology is rarely helpful beyond good and routine
cytologic assessment along with appropriate ultrasound and clinical interpretation. Second, ThinPrep by its very design eliminates extracellular debris to supposedly obtain a better look at the cytologic detail of the epithelial cells collected. While
this may be helpful in cervical/vaginal cytology interpretation, this means for thyroid interpretation you are eliminating colloid which is a key component in determining whether an aspirate should be viewed as benign or suspicious. Finally, there is a
tendency for ThinPrep to disperse epithelial cells, again, appropriate for cervical/vaginal assessment but challenging in the setting of thyroid cytology, since that will generate more dyscohesion, creating the possibility of a higher percentage of
atypical or suspicious aspiration interpretations.
The caveat in this case is the fact that your smears do contain a reasonable number of Hurthle cells without much in the way of colloid or degenerative changes. As such, I think, as mentioned, it is reasonable to flag this as suspicious and recommend
surgical intervention. I did give brief thought to the possibility of a Hurthle cell variant of medullary carcinoma due to some comet-like changes to the cells; however, the cell nuclei clearly have prominent cherry red nucleoli and are small without
nuclear atypia, so unless there is some compelling clinical evidence to suggest the possibility of medullary cancer, I think we are dealing with a Hurthle cell tumor which statistically is going to be benign. To that point, in our own database at Mayo
clinic, whenever we classify an aspirate as suspicious for Hurthle cell neoplasms, 90% of surgically excised nodules are neoplastic, and within this category about 15% are malignant. Conversely, 10% of excised nodules are hyperplastic which means that
our ability to distinguish malignancy from hyperplasia is limited (15% versus 10%, respectively).
TEST: Expert's second opinion, requested by ESJH pathologist Dr. Laura Stewart"

the large cells to be positive for CD20, CD10, BCL6, MYC (approximately 30% of cells are positive, variable intensity), and Ki 67 (>90% of cells are positive). The large lymphoid cells are negative for CD3, BCL2, and MUM1. CD21 highlights follicular
dendritic cell meshworks that closely correspond to the areas of large cells. Small lymphocytes in the background are almost exclusively T cells (CD3 positive).
Flow cytometry demonstrated an abnormal CD10+ B cell population that lacks detectable light chain expression (see flow cytometry report below). This finding is typical for a lymphoma, but is not diagnostic of malignancy as it can occasionally be
encountered in cases of florid follicular lymphoid hyperplasia. Molecular diagnostic studies to evaluate for clonal IGH, IGK, or BCL2 IGH rearrangements demonstrated polyclonal B cells (see PCR reports below). FISH studies to evaluate for MYC, BCL6, and
BCL2 IGH rearrangements were negative (see FISH report below). These normal PCR and FISH results further support the possibility that this lymphoid infiltrate could be reactive, but do not exclude the possibility of lymphoma.
If clinically indicated, a larger biopsy that better demonstrates the tissue architecture is recommended to further clarify the nature of this atypical lymphoid infiltrate. The findings were discussed by telephone with Dr. Joanna Miragaya on 11/9/2016.
The case was reviewed at the Emory hematopathology consensus conference on 11/1/2016.

Comment	
Two H&E-stained slides (A1-1, B1-1), each with multiple tissue levels, are reviewed. Both slides demonstrate fragmented tumor cells that are organized into complex arborizing papillary structures with central fibrovascular cores. Psammomatous calcifications are admixed. Additional immunostains are performed on the provided outside block A1 at Emory. Tumor cells are TTF-1 and PAX8 positive. BRAF V600E is negative.
 
The provided clinical information of "multiple enlarged subcutaneous masses of right neck" is noted. Most likely, these represent metastatic tumor deposits within right lateral cervical lymph nodes. Fragments of native soft tissue are admixed in both blocks, but there is no definite evidence of lymph node architecture or of frank invasion of soft tissue structures. Additional immunostains performed at Emory focally demonstrate lesional cells surrounded by lymphoid stroma, supporting my impression of metastatic tumor deposits within cervical nodes.
 
Within the visualized material, lesional cells are compatible with classic type papillary thyroid carcinoma. There is no evidence of tumor necrosis, increased mitotic activity, or morphologic evidence of a named subtype of papillary thyroid carcinoma associated with a more aggressive clinical behavior (e.g. tall cell variant). Final morphologic typing is deferred to examination of an excisional/thyroidectomy specimen.
 
Pediatric papillary thyroid carcinomas have a higher frequency of non-BRAF V600E molecular alterations, including RET/PTC rearrangements and DICER1 mutations.

The provided immunostains show tumor cells to be positive for keratin MCK, CK7, synaptophysin, chromogranin A (focal), CD56, TTF-1, and calcitonin but negative for CK5/6, p63, S100, thyroglobulin, PSA, CDX-2, CD20, and CD3. A Ki67- stain shows a low

a primary lesion include larynx and lungs.

Best seen in the cellblock preparation are eosinophilic, columnar epithelial cells arranged in broken up follicular structures and even rare small papillary frond. Cells are negative for TTF-1 and only weak and focally positive for PAX8, both antibodies that typically strong and diffusely staining thyroid epithelial cells. Instead, cells stain with antibodies directed against p16 (moderate and diffuse) and PAX2 (very weak, yet a large subset). All other stains are negative, including synaptophysin, parathyroid hormone, estrogen receptor, GATA3, and NRAS Q61R and BRAF V600E.

Lack of GATA3 staining argues against breast cancer. Lack of synaptophysin staining argues against medullary thyroid carcinoma. Lack of the PTH staining argues against a parathyroid tumor.
